findings.claim: the financial-statement view of an engineering team systematically misclassifies the costs that actually drive the decisions.
findings.failure_mode: overstated extension of the financial-vs-managerial contrast
findings.evidence: Deep 13, 27: financial accounting reports historical results to external users; managerial accounting gives detailed, timely internal information. Source 1071-1072: financial accounting 'does not provide enough detailed information for the types of decisions made'. Nothing about misclassification.
findings.fix: correct: where the financial-statement view of an engineering team does not give the detail the decisions need (Ch 1.1; Ch 1.2).

findings.claim: (Source: Ch 10.6, "Make Decisions Using Constrained Resources") ... prioritising features by the ratio of revenue or strategic value to the engineering hours they consume
findings.failure_mode: non-existent section name; applied mapping swaps contribution margin for revenue
findings.evidence: Source 23101: section is 'Fundamentals of How to Make Decisions When Resources are Constrained'; no section 'Make Decisions Using Constrained Resources'. Deep 295 and source 23110-23114 rank by 'unit contribution margin per production restraint', not revenue.
findings.fix: correct: (Source: Ch 10.6, "Fundamentals of How to Make Decisions When Resources are Constrained"). For software, this maps onto prioritising features by the contribution (revenue less variable cost) they generate per engineering hour on the bottlenecked team or system, not by absolute revenue.

findings.claim: the first sale of a feature contributes nothing to fixed engineering cost; later sales accumulate contribution until break-even, after which each marginal sale flows to profit.
findings.failure_mode: misstates contribution-margin mechanics
findings.evidence: Deep 98: contribution margin is the per-unit contribution toward covering fixed costs; 'this $5 contribution margin is assumed to first cover fixed costs first and then realized as profit' [V]. Every unit, the first included, contributes its margin toward fixed cost.
findings.fix: correct: each sale contributes its contribution margin toward fixed engineering cost; once cumulative contribution covers fixed cost (break-even), each further sale's contribution is profit.

findings.claim: the Big-Three-autos pattern that the volume cites translates into the temptation to defend engineering headcount by allocating overhead to "the platform" or "the product" rather than naming the truly fixed engineering cost as a period cost.
findings.failure_mode: analogy misstates the source's mechanism
findings.evidence: Deep 158, 160: the Big Three pattern is overproduction, because absorption costing parks fixed overhead in unsold inventory, lowering unit cost and raising reported income. Headcount allocation with no inventory is a different mechanism.
findings.fix: correct: For software, the absorption-costing lesson is narrower: where engineering cost is capitalised into an asset rather than expensed, reported income can look better than the decision economics; use variable-cost (contribution) views for internal decisions (Ch 6.5).

findings.claim: (Source: Ch 10.2, "Identify and Apply Basic Methods of Cost Accounting for Special Order Decisions")
findings.failure_mode: non-existent section name
findings.evidence: Source 21961, 22404: Ch 10.2 is 'Evaluate and Determine Whether to Accept or Reject a Special Order', subsection 'Fundamentals of the Decision to Accept or Reject a Special Order'.
findings.fix: correct: (Source: Ch 10.2, "Fundamentals of the Decision to Accept or Reject a Special Order")

findings.claim: relevant-cost for under-twelve-month
findings.failure_mode: supported by source, absent from deep
findings.evidence: Deep 17, 265: short-term decisions are operational, no time bound. Source 22090 (Ch 10.1): 'usually 12 months or fewer'.
findings.fix: cycle-to-deep: Ch 10.1 'Identify Relevant Information for Decision-Making': short-term decisions impact the company 'in the short term, usually 12 months or fewer' [V].

findings.claim: What is the variable cost per incident ... versus the fixed cost of the reliability investment? At what incident rate does the investment break even? Apply CVP analysis as the volume develops it (Ch 3.2).
findings.failure_mode: analogy presented as the volume's own method
findings.evidence: Deep 104-110: the volume's break-even is sales volume at which contribution margin per unit sold covers fixed cost. An avoided-incident-cost break-even is a cost-avoidance comparison the volume does not develop.
findings.fix: correct: Apply a break-even comparison by analogy with CVP (Ch 3.2): fixed investment divided by avoided cost per incident gives the break-even incident count.

findings.claim: Variable cost only is right with excess capacity; full cost or market price is right at capacity.
findings.failure_mode: at-capacity rule absent from deep (which says no single solution); 'full cost' not the source's at-capacity answer
findings.evidence: Deep 259: with excess capacity, selling internally at variable cost benefits the company; 'the text develops the trade-offs but does not prescribe a single solution'. Source 20850-20851: market-based transfer pricing is 'very common' when the seller is at full capacity; 20953: with no excess capacity the transfer price 'should take into consideration the opportunity cost lost'.
findings.fix: cycle-to-deep: Ch 9.4 'Application of Transfer Pricing': market-based transfer pricing is common when the seller is at full capacity; with no excess capacity the transfer price should consider the opportunity cost of lost outside sales. Then correct: With excess capacity, transfer at variable cost benefits the company; at full capacity the transfer price should cover the opportunity cost of lost external sales, which is why market price is common there.

findings.claim: The IMA eight-step ethics framework (Ch 1.4) and the SOX whistleblower-protection framing (Ch 1.4) anchor the decision-rights of post-incident response. SOX Section 302 (CEO/CFO sign-off) creates accountability hooks above engineering.
findings.failure_mode: eight steps misattributed to the IMA; SOX 302 applied outside its scope
findings.evidence: Deep 45 / source 2488-2501: the eight steps are the volume's own outline, not the IMA's (deep 41: IMA's four standards). Deep 43: SOX Section 302 requires CEO and CFO to review and sign financial reports; it does not reach engineering incidents.
findings.fix: correct: The volume's eight-step outline for ethical issues (Ch 1.4) and SOX's whistleblower protections (Section 806, Ch 1.4) bear on post-incident disclosure. SOX Section 302 applies where an incident affects financial reports the CEO and CFO sign. (Line 130: 'IMA eight-step' -> 'eight-step'.)

findings.claim: Pricing turns on contribution margin per unit and break-even volume, not on cost-plus.
findings.failure_mode: position against cost-plus that the volume does not take
findings.evidence: Deep 68: for merchandisers, purchase cost plus mark-up determines the selling price. Deep 110: target pricing combines market analysis 'with a markup percentage'. The volume takes no stance against cost-plus pricing.
findings.fix: correct: Pricing decisions need contribution margin per unit and break-even volume alongside any markup.

findings.claim: Theory-of-Constraints framing: speed and quality are not in symmetric tension; one is usually the constraint and the other a non-constraint.
findings.failure_mode: claim attributed to TOC (Ch 1.5) that the source does not make
findings.evidence: Deep 53 / source 2850-2892: TOC removes bottlenecks in the value chain (physical, policy, culture, market constraints, Table 1.5) through five steps. Nothing treats speed or quality as constraints or addresses their tension.
findings.fix: correct: Theory-of-Constraints framing (Ch 1.5): find the bottleneck that limits delivery (a team, a review gate, a test stage) and work it through identify, exploit, subordinate, elevate, repeat. The standard-cost-variance warning applies: ...

findings.claim: Follow-up: rank by contribution-margin-per-bottleneck-hour; expect the priority order to change.
findings.failure_mode: overclaim
findings.evidence: Deep 295: the highest-contribution-per-unit product 'may not be' the highest per constraint hour.
findings.fix: correct: ... the priority order may change.

findings.claim: 2 would actually be reassigned to higher-priority reliability work (saving $400K only in opportunity-cost terms; the headcount remains) ... The avoidable in-house cost is $200K (hosting only); the vendor cost is $480K. Build, not buy.
findings.failure_mode: worked example drops a relevant opportunity cost, reversing the decision
findings.evidence: Deep 273: opportunity cost is 'the costs associated with not choosing the other alternative'; the distillation's own Key Concept 2 (line 18) says opportunity costs are typically relevant. Deep 283 (Table 10.2): buying 'frees up capacity for other uses'. Counting the $400K the example names, build's relevant cost is $600K against $480K buy.
findings.fix: correct: Of the 5 engineers, 2 would move to higher-priority reliability work if CloudForge buys; their $400K is an opportunity cost of building and is relevant. Relevant build cost is $200K hosting plus $400K opportunity cost = $600K against the $480K licence. Buy, unless the 3 engineers who cannot be released make the stack cheaper to keep than the numbers show.

findings.claim: "A cost or revenue is relevant if it differs between alternatives. Sunk costs, unavoidable costs, and future costs that do not differ are irrelevant." ... the Thermal Mugs pattern the volume names: "whether $0.12 of allocated fixed cost is avoidable swings the decision."
findings.failure_mode: distillation's own wording presented as quotation of the volume
findings.evidence: Both strings are the distillation's Key Concepts 2 and 3 wording; source grep for 'A cost or revenue is relevant if it differs' and 'swings the decision': 0 hits. Content traces to deep 267-273, 281.
findings.fix: correct: drop the quotation marks and 'the volume names'; paraphrase with citation, or copy an audited [V] passage from the deep ref (e.g. the Ch 10.1 sunk-cost sentence) as a blockquote.

findings.claim: The volume's Theory of Constraints five-step applies directly: "identifying the single binding constraint, exploiting it, subordinating everything else to it, elevating it, and repeating." ... Combined analysis: payback under four quarters on direct cost
findings.failure_mode: self-quotation presented as the volume's words; payback figure contradicts the example's own arithmetic
findings.evidence: Quoted string is Key Concept 4's wording; source 2876-2889 lists the steps as 'Identify the system constraint. Decide how best to exploit the constraint ... Subordinate everything else ... Elevate the system's constraint ... Repeat the process.' The example computes 12 engineer-weeks / 3 per quarter = payback in four quarters, not under.
findings.fix: correct: The volume's five TOC steps apply (Ch 1.5): identify the system constraint, exploit it, subordinate everything else, elevate it, repeat. ... Combined analysis: payback in four quarters on direct cost

findings.claim: IRR: approximately 14 per cent, modestly above the hurdle. ... The volume's capital-budgeting discipline: "Capital decisions involve large outlays, long horizons, and the time value of money; payback and ARR are screens; NPV and IRR are the substantive tools."
findings.failure_mode: arithmetic error; self-quotation presented as the volume's words
findings.evidence: Required 5-year annuity factor = 4.8 / 1.5 = 3.200; the 16% factor is 3.274 and 17% is 3.199, so IRR is about 17%. (At 14% the factor 3.433 gives PV $5.15M > $4.8M, so IRR must exceed 14%.) The quoted sentence is Key Concept 8's wording; not in source.
findings.fix: correct: IRR: approximately 17 per cent, above the 12 per cent hurdle. ... The volume treats payback and ARR as screening tools and NPV and IRR as the time-value methods (Ch 11.2; Ch 11.4).

findings.claim: The volume's position: "Financial measures alone are insufficient"
findings.failure_mode: paraphrase presented as quotation
findings.evidence: The string is the deep ref's thesis paraphrase (deep 19, unmarked); source grep: 0 hits. Deep 367 carries a [V] Ch 12.4 passage that would serve.
findings.fix: correct: The volume's position is that financial measures alone evaluate the past and can be gamed (Ch 12.1; Ch 12.4). Or blockquote deep 367: "The combination of these different types of quantitative and qualitative measures ... enables an organization to more adequately assess how it is progressing toward meeting short- and long-term goals." [V] (Ch 12.4)

findings.claim: The volume's decision-relative cost classification — "fixed for what decision? avoidable for what alternative? sunk relative to which forward question?" — runs underneath all four. (Source: Ch 2.2 ...)
findings.failure_mode: distillation's own heuristic presented as quotation from Ch 2.2
findings.evidence: Source grep 'fixed for what decision': 0 hits. Deep 76 carries the audited [V] Ch 2.2 passage: 'in practice, the classification of costs changes as the use of the cost data changes ...'
findings.fix: correct: drop the quotation marks, or blockquote deep 76: "in practice, the classification of costs changes as the use of the cost data changes. In fact, a single cost, such as rent, may be classified by one company as a fixed cost, by another company as a committed cost, and by even another company as a period cost" [V] (Ch 2.2).

findings.claim: Allocating fixed engineering cost to products to defend headcount or platform investment is the Big-Three-autos pattern in software shape
findings.failure_mode: analogy misstates the source's mechanism (see D004)
findings.evidence: Deep 158, 160: the Big Three pattern is overproduction into inventory under absorption costing.
findings.fix: correct: Using absorption-style figures (fixed cost spread over units or capitalised) to judge internal decisions hides the fixed-cost impact; the volume prescribes variable costing for internal decisions, absorption only for external reporting (Ch 6.5).

findings.claim: The J&J Tylenol pattern ... is the volume's case-study contrast to the Bhopal pattern (Ch 13.1).
findings.failure_mode: framing the source does not use
findings.evidence: Deep 382-386 / source 28940-28950: Union Carbide, Nestlé and J&J are 'three featured cases' that drove sustainability reporting, presented in sequence, not as a contrast pair.
findings.fix: correct: The J&J Tylenol case (protect people first, then the product; the recall cost more than $100 million and the share price recovered within six weeks) is one of the volume's three featured crisis cases, alongside Union Carbide's Bhopal disaster (Ch 13.1).

findings.claim: Letaw structures the engineering work and the decision rights ... The microservices boundary case in Letaw and the make-or-buy analysis in Ch 10.3 here both turn on the same question: where do the cost and decision boundaries actually fall?
findings.failure_mode: decision-rights and cost-boundary framing not in Letaw's deep ref
findings.evidence: letaw-handbook-sweng-methods-deep: no decision-rights content (grep 'decision right': 0). Ch 5 (189-205) treats monolith vs microservices as architecture: independence, business-capability organisation, decentralised data and governance. No cost analysis.
findings.fix: correct: Letaw structures the engineering work and its methods ... Letaw's monolith-versus-microservices chapter (independently replaceable services, decentralised governance) and this volume's make-or-buy analysis (Ch 10.3) can be read together when a component boundary is also a sourcing decision.

findings.claim: Flow economics over utilisation is the lean theme that Ch 1.5 references and Goldratt's TOC develops; Kanban operationalises the same theme at the team level. ... Kanban's WIP-limit and constraint-management discipline.
findings.failure_mode: theme attributed to Ch 1.5 and to Open Kanban that neither deep ref carries
findings.evidence: Deep 53: Ch 1.5 covers TQM, JIT, LSS, kaizen and TOC; no flow-versus-utilisation theme. open-kanban-deep: 'utilisation'/'utilization' 0 hits, 'bottleneck' 0 hits; it cites Lean/TPS and Goldratt's TOC as lineage (52, 131) and treats limiting WIP as a consequence of batch-size reduction (74-76).
findings.fix: correct: | Open Kanban | Ch 1.5 presents lean practices and Goldratt's TOC; Open Kanban cites Lean/TPS and Goldratt's TOC (with Deming) as lineage and treats limiting WIP as a consequence of reducing batch size. The volume's contribution-margin-per-constraint ranking (Ch 10.6) is a financial complement to Kanban's flow discipline. |

findings.claim: The five responsibility-centre types align with Mintzberg's organisational structures
findings.failure_mode: concept attributed to Mintzberg that the Principles of Management deep does not carry
findings.evidence: openstax-principles-management-deep: Mintzberg appears for managerial work and three role clusters (15, 29, 33-37, 780-782), not organisational structures. Structures (functional, divisional, geographic, 187-193) carry no Mintzberg attribution.
findings.fix: correct: The five responsibility-centre types sit alongside Principles of Management's functional, divisional and geographic structures; its divisional structure's decentralised decision-making parallels this volume's Ch 9.1 treatment of decentralisation.

findings.claim: Goldratt — cited as the foundational framework for the five-step TOC focusing cycle and the constraint-management argument running through Ch 1.5 and Ch 10.6.

findings.claim: The deep reference carries the volume's load-bearing claims with [V] markers (the five-step TOC focusing cycle; the contribution-margin-per-bottleneck-unit formulation; ... the balanced scorecard four-perspective description; the Ford Pinto cost-benefit framing; the J&J Tylenol and Bhopal case contrast). ... no verbatim blockquotes appear here. The eight-step ethics framework is [AP] ... consistent with the deep ref's evidence classification.
findings.failure_mode: marker claims do not match the deep ref or the distillation
findings.evidence: Deep 53 (TOC five steps), 295 (CM per constraint), 55 and 356-361 (BSC perspectives), 297 and 527 (Ford Pinto), 384-386 (Bhopal, Tylenol) carry no [V]; only the variable/absorption definitions (156) are [V]. Deep 45 gives the eight steps unmarked, not [AP]. Distillation line 32 carries two [V] quotations (both match source 22235-22237).
findings.fix: correct: The deep ref marks [V] the definitions of variable and absorption costing (Ch 6.5), the sunk-cost sentence (Ch 10.1), and the TOC definition (Ch 1.5); the TOC steps, constraint ranking, BSC perspectives, Ford Pinto and crisis cases are carried as paraphrase or unmarked quotation. This distillation carries two [V] quotations (Key Concept 9) and otherwise paraphrases. The eight-step outline is the volume's own and unmarked in the deep ref.

notes: The two [V] quotations (line 32: 'have no bearing on future events and are not relevant in decision-making'; 'due to human nature') match the converted source (22235-22237). Chapter titles cited in line 10 match the source (Ch 3 'Cost-Volume-Profit Analysis', Ch 10 'Short-Term Decision Making', Ch 11 'Capital Budgeting Decisions', Ch 12 'Balanced Scorecard and Other Performance Measures', Ch 13 'Sustainability Reporting'). Worked-example arithmetic checked: Decision 1 $1.2M in-house; Decision 3 payback 3.2 yrs, PV ~$5.41M, PI 1.13 correct; IRR wrong (D016). The worked example carries five quotation-marked strings, none from the source (D014-D018); the scope is open-nc and the protocol asks for 2-5 audited [V] blockquotes, of which the example has none. Lens sections: the business-executive lens (line 219) places the sustainability-reporting choice in 'Phase 5', but Phase 5 here is risk/reliability/compliance and the GRI/SASB choice sits in Key Concept 15 and Phase 6; internal cross-reference, not a source claim. Integration rows for Scrum+AP Field Guide (velocity, capacity-adjusted velocity from APFG deep 78-115), Principles of Marketing (segmentation, value-based pricing), Principles of Finance, Business Law (contract, consumer protection), Entrepreneurship (pivot, funding stages) and NHS/TC 25-20 check out against those deep refs.
